description:
A potential early Christian church identifed due to its unique architectural layout and orientation. It features a east-west alignment and a plan consisting of a central nave flanked by two aisles, a configuration that is unparalleled by any other structure found within the town. Its identification as a religious site is further supported by the 1970s discovery of the Water Newton Treasure nearby, which contained early Christian liturgical silver. Additionally, unlike most other buildings at Durobrivae, this structure was not systematically robbed of its stone, suggesting it remained in use longer than surrounding buildings or was held in high enough regard to be protected from dismantling.

Regarding its positioning and chronology, the building is situated in the southwestern part of the town and appears to partially overlie the outer ditch of a large circular feature referred to as a "tumulus". This circular feature is believed to be a prehistoric monument, and the positioning of the church over it may suggest an emerging interest in pre-Roman monuments, paralleled at many other sites. While no precise founding date was established, the pottery recovered from the trench was predominantly from the late 3rd and 4th centuries AD. The building’s survival in an unrobbed state and its association with late-Roman Christian artifacts indicate that it was likely an active focal point of the community during the final phases of Roman Durobrivae.
